claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by an interplay between additive-manufacturing-induced microstructural heterogeneities and selective oxidation or reduction reactions.
The additive manufacturing process produces directional grain boundaries and residual stresses in the alloy.
Under oxidizing conditions, Al and Cr become locally enriched at exposed grain boundaries.
Local Al and Cr enrichment promotes formation of a transient, partially protective oxide scale.
The oxide scale eventually spalls because of poor adhesion and mismatch with the substrate stress state.
Under reducing atmospheres, the protective surface scale is absent or unstable.
In reducing atmospheres, AM-induced inhomogeneities provide fast diffusion paths that enhance internal oxidation.
Enhanced internal oxidation in reducing atmospheres produces uniform, gradual degradation.
The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy has directional grain structure and potential residual stresses inherited from additive manufacturing.
Oxide-scale formation, composition, and stability are mediated by grain boundaries and residual stresses.
Thermal-expansion mismatch and microstructural stress concentrations compromise adhesion of the Al- and Cr-containing scale.
Oxidizing exposure will initially cause weight gain and formation of a fine oxide scale.
The oxide formed under oxidizing exposure will subsequently spall at locations correlated with microstructural features.
Reducing exposure will produce more uniform internal oxidation and less visible surface scale than oxidizing exposure.
Reducing exposure will cause measurable hardness loss and changes in microstructural integrity relative to the as-built state.
The as-manufactured baseline has minimal pre-existing oxide scale.
The proposed mechanism applies above approximately 800 °C for exposures of at least 10 hours in strongly oxidizing or strongly reducing atmospheres.
A 900 °C, 20-hour comparison between air and 5% H2 in an inert gas can distinguish the predicted degradation modes.
Failure to observe both atmosphere-dependent degradation modes and correlation with AM-induced microstructural features would reject the hypothesis.
